kept.title: Harden the existing tool-call path for Gemma-4-26B-A4B on vLLM before switching frameworks: official chat template, matching parsers and loop guards
kept.what_to_change: (a) Relaunch Gemma with vLLM's official tool chat template and matching parsers: --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --chat-template <vllm>/examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja --enable-prefix-caching. The template ships in the vLLM repo's examples/ directory, so check that the copy matches your vLLM 0.31 build. (b) Run a three-stage tool-call test: one tool call alone, then the full tool schema plus the Open WebUI system prompt, then the full agent loop. If stages 1 and 2 pass but stage 3 fails, the framework is the problem, not the model. (c) In the Telegram bot's agent loop, add the guards recommended for Gemma 4: cap retries per step at 2, suppress a tool call that repeats the previous one with the same arguments, and never write a malformed tool-call turn back into history (replace it with a short correction instruction, or abort). (d) A/B test MTP on and off, and streaming against stream:false, for tool-call turns only. Community reports link malformed Gemma 4 calls to speculative decoding and to streaming deltas. Keep MTP on for the final, tool-free answer turn, where it gives most of the speed.
kept.expected_gain: Fewer broken multi-step runs: no lost tool parameters, no reasoning or tool text leaking into the chat, no loops. This is probably the single biggest reliability gain for the least effort. It costs no extra memory, and the speed cost is limited to tool turns if MTP or streaming has to be turned off there.
evidence: ai-muninn.com DGX Spark part 15 (https://ai-muninn.com/en/blog/swe-bench-local-models-framework-matters): Gemma 4 26B-A4B NVFP4 on GB10 lost tool-call parameters unless the official vLLM tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja was supplied. In OpenHands v0.59 it needed 4 to 40+ attempts before its first successful call (parsers tried: pythonic, hermes, gemma4), yet it fixed the same bug in 9 steps in SWE-agent v1.1.0, so the action format mattered more than the model.

HF forum 'Gemma 4 bug fixes and Research Request' (https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/gemma-4-bug-fixes-and-research-request/176979): with long context plus reasoning, Gemma 4 emits malformed tool calls and then imitates them once they are fed back into history. Suggested mitigations: disable MTP or speculative decoding for tool calls, use stream:false, never feed malformed turns back, cap retries.

vLLM issue #39043: reasoning or tool-call text leaks into chat with --reasoning-parser gemma4 --tool-call-parser gemma4. vLLM issue #42696: the streaming gemma4 parser sends id, type and name only on the first chunk, which breaks clients that validate every chunk.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies directly. Gemma-4-26B-A4B NVFP4 with MTP is our default model, and both Open WebUI native tool calling (server-side loop) and the Telegram bot's own loop use the same vLLM endpoint. Open WebUI's docs say the fix for a model that struggles in Native mode is a better tool-calling model or setup, not Legacy mode.
kept.risk: Low. Restarting vLLM interrupts service for a few minutes. If you disable MTP on tool turns, decode on those turns drops from about 50 tok/s toward the non-MTP rate, which I did not measure. The template must match the vLLM build, or tool calls may break in a different way.
kept.test_plan: Write 25 fixed Uzbek multi-step tasks, for example: get the CBU dollar rate, then calculate X, then write the result to an Excel file; search, then fetch 2 pages, then summarize; run an SQL query, then make a chart. Run each 3 times before and after the change through both Open WebUI (/api/chat/completions with chat_id, streaming) and the Telegram loop. Record task success, malformed tool calls per run, retries, wall time and time to first token. Accept the change if malformed calls fall by at least 50% and success rises, with p50 latency no worse than +15%.
kept.verifier_reason: The core of this is sound. vLLM ships gemma4 tool and reasoning parsers and examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja for Gemma 4, the cited failure modes are consistent with known Gemma 4 issues, and the guards in the Telegram loop cost nothing. One part is wrong. In vLLM, speculative decoding (MTP) is set once per server through --speculative-config, so it cannot be switched off for tool turns and kept on for the final answer turn. Doing that would need two Gemma servers, which does not fit in about 15 GiB. stream:false, by contrast, is a per-request setting, so it can be used on tool turns only. --enable-prefix-caching is already on by default in the vLLM V1 engine, so adding it is harmless but gains nothing. Before applying the template, check that it matches the 0.31 build.
kept.corrected_change: (a) Relaunch with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --chat-template using the tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja from the same vLLM 0.31 tag. Prefix caching is already the default. (b) Keep the three-stage diagnosis: one tool call, then the full schema, then the full loop. (c) Add the loop guards: at most 2 retries per step, drop a call identical to the previous one, never write a malformed turn back into history, and cap the run at about 8 steps. (d) In the Telegram loop and the Open WebUI requests, use stream:false on tool turns as a per-request A/B. Test MTP on against MTP off only as a whole-server A/B, measuring malformed calls against the overall tok/s loss. If MTP turns out to cause the malformed calls, prefer the guards and keep MTP on, rather than running two Gemma servers.

kept.title: Pilot Hermes Agent (Nous Research, NVIDIA's DGX Spark playbook, v0.18.0 / 2026.7.1 or later) as a second runtime for Telegram and as a 'hermes-agent' model in Open WebUI, with a trimmed toolset
kept.what_to_change: Install it next to the current stack without replacing anything: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash. In the setup wizard choose Blank Slate, a custom endpoint, Local terminal backend, and everything disabled. Then run: hermes config set model.provider custom; hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8000/v1; hermes config set model.default <served model id>; hermes -z "Reply exactly HERMES_OK". Next, cut the bootstrap prompt by listing unneeded toolsets under agent.disabled_toolsets in ~/.hermes/config.yaml and keeping skills to a minimum. Write an Uzbek persona in ~/.hermes/SOUL.md. Set compression.threshold to 0.5 and leave auxiliary.compression.model empty, so the main model does the summarizing and nothing extra is loaded into memory. Expose the existing SearXNG, CBU and SQL tools to Hermes as MCP servers (mcp_servers block) rather than rewriting them. For Telegram: run hermes gateway setup with a new test bot token and an allow-list of your numeric user ID, and keep the production python-telegram-bot running in parallel. For Open WebUI: hermes config set API_SERVER_ENABLED true, set API_SERVER_KEY, run hermes gateway (it listens on 127.0.0.1:8642), and in Open WebUI add an OpenAI connection to http://host.docker.internal:8642/v1 with that key, which adds a 'hermes-agent' model to the picker.
kept.expected_gain: Hermes is a maintained agent loop that is already built for Telegram and OpenAI-compatible frontends. It adds memory, session search, self-written skills, subagents, cron and context compression, so we would maintain less custom loop code. NVIDIA tested it on DGX Spark against a local vLLM endpoint. Gains in reliability and speed for Uzbek tasks are unproven and must be measured.
evidence: NVIDIA DGX Spark playbook (https://build.nvidia.com/spark/hermes-agent/instructions): verified against Hermes Agent v0.18.0 (2026.7.1); uses local vLLM at http://localhost:8000/v1; the recipe sets --max-model-len 262144; the Telegram gateway is set up via hermes gateway setup with an allowed-user list and a systemd service.

Hermes API server docs (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/api-server): /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses and /v1/runs with SSE tool events; tools run server-side; X-Hermes-Session-Id for continuing transcripts; max_concurrent_runs defaults to 10; accepts only inline images, no file uploads.

Hermes Open WebUI guide (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/open-webui): streaming shows tool progress inline; Open WebUI still sends full history; long responses can appear all at once when the agent finishes. The docs do not say whether Open WebUI's own tools are passed through, and Hermes uses its own toolset.

Community reports (r/hermesagent, fast.io guide): local models feel slow because Hermes sends a large bootstrap prompt (system prompt plus 40+ tool schemas) on every turn. The suggested workaround is to disable toolsets and memory and use minimal profiles. These are user opinions, not official guidance.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Partially. It speaks the same OpenAI vLLM endpoint and needs no new GPU memory, since it is only a Python process. It could replace or augment the Telegram bot's own loop. In Open WebUI it would appear as a separate model, but Open WebUI's custom tools, RAG and memory would not be available inside Hermes runs; port the tools as MCP. Prefill cost is the main concern on GB10: one forum thread reports 150 to 600 tok/s prefill for the 35B-A3B NVFP4 model, so a 15k-token tool bootstrap could add tens of seconds on a cold cache. --enable-prefix-caching and a stable system prompt are essential.
kept.risk: Medium. The prompt is large and the first turn may be slower than our current loop. The docs disagree internally (for example on the Idempotency-Key retention window). The code changes fast (around 52k commits and no tagged releases on GitHub). The terminal tool runs on the host, so keep the Local backend inside a sandbox user or use the Docker backend. Never expose 8642 or 8000 to the LAN without authentication. All this is single-user, and Hermes defaults to a 10-run concurrency cap.
kept.test_plan: Run the same 25-task Uzbek suite from recommendation 1 through Hermes on Telegram (test bot) and through the Open WebUI 'hermes-agent' model, against the current bot and Open WebUI Native mode, on the same model. Record success rate, steps, total prompt tokens per task (from the vLLM /metrics prompt_tokens counters), time to first token and wall time. Also measure the bootstrap prompt size per turn before and after setting disabled_toolsets. Adopt Hermes for Telegram only if success is at least 10 percentage points higher, or equal with 30% less code to maintain, and p50 wall time is no more than 1.3x the current loop.
kept.verifier_reason: Hermes Agent is a real Nous Research project, and NVIDIA's Spark playbook runs it against a local vLLM endpoint. It is a CPU-side Python process, so it uses no extra GPU memory. Three things need fixing. The install step pipes curl from the main branch straight into bash on the host, which is unsafe and not reproducible, so pin a version instead. The risk section's 'no tagged releases' contradicts the v0.18.0 version it cites. The expected gain for one user is speculative: it brings in a large bootstrap prompt, and inside Open WebUI it loses Open WebUI's own tools, RAG and memory. It is worth a pilot for Telegram only, and only after the eval harness and recommendation 1 are done.
kept.corrected_change: Install a pinned release (the v0.18.0 / 2026.7.1 the playbook verified) under a dedicated unprivileged user or the Docker terminal backend, not curl|bash from main as your own user. Pilot it on Telegram only first, with a test bot and an allow-list. Port SearXNG, CBU and SQL as MCP servers, set disabled_toolsets, and keep the main model for compression. Measure the bootstrap prompt in tokens and the TTFT on the first turn and on later prefix-cached turns. Add the Open WebUI 'hermes-agent' connection only if the Telegram pilot passes the gate set in the eval harness. Bind ports 8642 and 8000 to 127.0.0.1 only.

kept.title: Split agent turns by model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 runs the tool loop, Gemma-4 writes the final Uzbek answer and handles vision
kept.what_to_change: Serve nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4, the model NVIDIA's playbook names as agent-ready for Spark, with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder (qwen3_xml is a fallback) --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-prefix-caching, and a max-model-len that fits memory (64k to 128k rather than 262k). If the reasoning parser swallows output, leaving an empty answer, test without it. Because only about 15 GiB is free, the Qwen3.6 server should replace the Qwen3.8-27B 'Pro' server rather than run as a third model. Route the work as follows. In the Telegram bot, and in Hermes (recommendation 2), plan and call tools with Qwen3.6, with internal tool reasoning in English. When the loop ends, hand the collected tool results to Gemma-4-26B-A4B with an instruction to write the user-facing answer in Uzbek. Images still go to Gemma. In Open WebUI, put the same split in a Pipe function (a generator with __event_emitter__ status events).
kept.expected_gain: Tool steps run at about 110 to 134 tok/s instead of about 50 (Gemma) or 25 (Qwen3.8-27B), so each multi-step task finishes noticeably faster, while answer quality in Uzbek stays at Gemma's level. Qwen3.x MoE models with qwen3_coder parsing appear to be the most reliable at structured tool calls on Spark in community testing.
evidence: NVIDIA Hermes and vLLM playbooks (https://build.nvidia.com/spark/hermes-agent/agent-ready-models.md): the only agent-ready model listed for DGX Spark is nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4. The page gives no benchmarks.
vLLM Qwen3.5/3.6 recipe (docs.vllm.ai/projects/recipes, Qwen3.5): for tool calling, --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-prefix-caching --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder.

ai-muninn DGX Spark part 15: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B FP8 completed the OpenHands task with 1 recoverable error where Gemma 4 failed. The same source warns that --reasoning-parser qwen3 consumed all output as thinking (empty response) and recommends qwen3_xml. In SWE-agent, Qwen ran 96 steps and never submitted, so it needs a step cap.

Third-party aggregators: the dense Qwen3.6-27B beats 35B-A3B on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (59.3 vs 51.5) and SWE-bench Verified (77.2 vs 73.4), so the MoE model trades some capability for about 4x the speed.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies directly. The model is already downloaded, and our own observation that it is weaker at Uzbek multi-step tasks is the reason to keep Gemma for the final Uzbek wording. Memory: the NVFP4 35B-A3B weights are about 20 GB or more plus KV cache, so it cannot coexist with Gemma, Qwen3.8-27B, bge-m3 and the reranker inside the 15 GiB headroom. One of the existing models has to go.
kept.risk: Medium. The handoff between two models adds one extra prefill of the tool results on Gemma. Uzbek entity names and numbers can be garbled when Qwen extracts them. Dropping the 27B Pro model removes the slow but strongest option. Disagreement over parser flags (qwen3_coder vs qwen3_xml, reasoning parser on or off) needs testing on vLLM 0.31.
kept.test_plan: On the 25-task suite, compare three set-ups: Gemma alone, Qwen3.6 alone, and Qwen3.6 for the loop with Gemma for the answer. Record success, malformed calls, wall time, and a blind 1-to-5 rating of the Uzbek answers from the user. Check memory with nvidia-smi and free -g during runs. Adopt the split if success is at least equal to Gemma alone, the Uzbek rating is no more than 0.3 lower, and p50 wall time is at least 30% lower.
kept.verifier_reason: The parts exist: an NVFP4 checkpoint of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the qwen3_coder and qwen3_xml parsers, and the qwen3 reasoning parser. Swapping it in for the 27B Pro server roughly fits memory, but only if --gpu-memory-utilization is set so the two vLLM servers do not over-claim unified memory. The claimed gain is overstated. Tool-step turns are short and dominated by prefill, so a 2 to 2.5x decode speed-up does not shorten wall time by the same factor. The handoff also adds an uncached prefill of the tool results on Gemma. The bigger risk is the user's own observation that Qwen3.6 is weaker on Uzbek multi-step tasks. The hard part, understanding the Uzbek request and planning the tool calls, would move to the weaker model. Keep it as a gated experiment, not as an adoption.
kept.corrected_change: Run it only as an A/B in the eval harness. Serve Qwen3.6-35B-A3B NVFP4 in place of the 27B Pro server, with an explicit --gpu-memory-utilization and --max-model-len of 32k to 64k. Use --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder, falling back to qwen3_xml, and test the qwen3 reasoning parser both on and off on vLLM 0.31. Set max_steps to about 8. Pass the original Uzbek user message, verbatim, to both the Qwen loop and the Gemma final answer, and keep numbers and entity names as raw tool output rather than as Qwen's paraphrase. Adopt the split only if success is at least equal to Gemma alone and p50 wall time drops by at least 25%. Keep the 27B weights on disk so it can be rolled back.

kept.title: Pick by integration fit: skip OpenHands, Goose and opencode as the assistant runtime; prototype smolagents CodeAgent only for research and data tasks
kept.what_to_change: Do not adopt OpenHands, Goose or opencode as Sarob's main runtime. They are coding agents built around workspaces, heavy JSON tool schemas, and in OpenHands' case Docker sandboxes, and none of them is designed to serve Telegram or Open WebUI chat. For the jobs that suit code (deep research, data and Excel work, SQL plus a chart), prototype a smolagents CodeAgent (pip install smolagents, current 1.2x) using OpenAIServerModel(api_base='http://localhost:8000/v1'). Have it run Python in the existing Jupyter or Open Terminal sandbox, with our tools wrapped as @tool functions. Expose it as a single Open WebUI tool or Pipe, 'kod_agent', and as a Telegram command. Write it max_steps=8 and emit status events. Reach for LangGraph only if we need deterministic, resumable workflows. A LangGraph Pipe exists on the Open WebUI marketplace (pessini/langgraph_hitl), but it means building and maintaining the graph ourselves.
kept.expected_gain: CodeAgent's code actions avoid filling in JSON tool forms, which is the format Gemma 4 handles worst. The smolagents authors claim about 30% fewer steps and LLM calls than JSON tool calls. Keeping the heavier frameworks out avoids a lot of integration work that would gain nothing for a chat assistant.
evidence: ai-muninn DGX Spark part 15: Gemma 4 failed OpenHands' JSON function-calling format (11 tools, an 8,892-character system prompt) but succeeded with SWE-agent's text and code action format. Their summary: Gemma 4 can code but cannot fill out JSON forms reliably.

smolagents README (github.com/huggingface/smolagents): CodeAgent 'uses 30% fewer steps (thus 30% fewer LLM calls)' and scores higher on hard benchmarks. This is a vendor claim from before 2026, and I found no vLLM or 2026 study of it.
vLLM issue #42696: opencode's @ai-sdk client validates every streamed chunk and aborts on vLLM's streaming gemma4 tool parser output.

Goose / AAIF blog 2026 and Goose's 2025 benchmark: small local models' tool calling depends on the combination of model, host and prompt format, and tool-shimmed models score lower. Goose is MCP-first and aimed at the desktop or CLI, not Telegram.
Open WebUI docs (pipes.md, events.md): Pipes can stream from a generator and emit status events through __event_emitter__, which is how an external agent can be shown in chat.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: smolagents fits well. Jupyter and Open Terminal already provide the sandbox, the tools are plain Python, and it needs no new model or GPU memory. The coding agents fit poorly for a single-user Uzbek chat assistant.
kept.risk: Low to medium. Code execution needs a sandbox, never the host Python. CodeAgent prompts are long, which raises prefill cost. The 30% claim may not hold for Gemma or Qwen in Uzbek.
kept.test_plan: Take the 10 data and research tasks from the suite. Run smolagents CodeAgent and ToolCallingAgent against Open WebUI Native mode on the same Gemma endpoint, 3 runs each. Record success, LLM calls and wall time. Keep CodeAgent only if success is equal or better with at least 20% fewer calls.
kept.verifier_reason: Rejecting the coding-agent frameworks as a chat runtime is correct. smolagents is real and pip-installable on aarch64 (pure Python), and its OpenAIServerModel works against vLLM. One claim is wrong: smolagents' executors are local, e2b, docker, modal and wasm. It does not run code in an existing Jupyter or Open Terminal sandbox out of the box. In a remote executor, the @tool functions must also be shipped into that executor. The 30% figure is the authors' own claim and has not been checked on Gemma 4 in Uzbek.
kept.corrected_change: Prototype a smolagents CodeAgent using OpenAIServerModel(api_base='http://localhost:8000/v1'), with executor_type='docker' (aarch64 Python image, no network except the tool endpoints) or a small custom executor that posts code to the existing Jupyter kernel gateway. Never use the local executor on the host. Keep the tools as thin HTTP wrappers so they work inside the executor. Set max_steps to 8, emit status events through an Open WebUI Pipe, and judge it with the eval harness: keep it only if success is equal or better with at least 20% fewer LLM calls.

kept.title: Build a repeatable Uzbek agent eval harness so each runtime and model change is a measured decision
kept.what_to_change: Write a small Python script, eval_agents.py, that sends each of 25 to 30 fixed Uzbek multi-step tasks to: Open WebUI /api/chat/completions in Native mode (with chat_id and assistant message id, since otherwise only one tool round runs), the Telegram bot's loop function called directly, Hermes on :8642/v1, and smolagents. Check each answer with deterministic validators (expected CBU rate within a tolerance, expected SQL row count, file exists) and save JSONL with tokens, steps and timings. To track throughput, scrape vLLM /metrics before and after each run (prompt_tokens_total, generation_tokens_total, time_to_first_token). Run it nightly or after every config change.
kept.expected_gain: Turns the user's complaints ('slow', 'not smart enough') into numbers, so we can see which of recommendations 1 to 4 actually help instead of guessing. This matters because none of the sources I found includes Uzbek agent benchmarks.
evidence: Open WebUI server-side tool calling reference (https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/server-side-tool-calling): the full agent loop runs only when the request includes chat_id and an assistant message id and uses streaming; otherwise only one round of tools runs.
ai-muninn: the three-stage diagnosis (one call, full schema, full loop) separated framework failures from model failures on GB10.
No primary source covers agent reliability in Uzbek. All framework claims (Hermes, smolagents 30%, Goose) come from vendors or anecdotes.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies directly. It reuses our existing endpoints and tools, needs no GPU memory, and with one user runs can be scheduled at night.
kept.risk: Low. The main risk is tasks that drift as live data changes (exchange rates, search results). Validators must allow a tolerance, or freeze the source data in fixtures.
kept.test_plan: Pass condition for the harness itself: two consecutive runs on an unchanged config agree within ±5 percentage points on success rate and ±10% on p50 wall time. After that, use it as the decision gate for recommendations 1 to 4.
kept.verifier_reason: This uses only existing endpoints, needs no GPU memory and suits a single user. The prometheus metric names exist in vLLM's /metrics, with a vllm: prefix: prompt_tokens_total, generation_tokens_total and the time_to_first_token histogram. It is the prerequisite gate for recommendations 1 to 4, so it should come first in order, not fifth.
kept.corrected_change: Do this first, before recommendations 1 to 4. Write eval_agents.py with 25 to 30 Uzbek tasks, and freeze or record the fixtures for live data such as the CBU rate and search results. Use deterministic validators. Send Open WebUI requests with chat_id, the assistant message id and stream:true. Scrape vllm:prompt_tokens_total, vllm:generation_tokens_total and vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds from /metrics before and after each run, and write results to JSONL. Run it twice on an unchanged config to confirm repeatability (±5 percentage points on success, ±10% on p50) before using it to decide anything.

kept.title: Do not migrate engines: keep vLLM as the only serving engine and treat SGLang, TRT-LLM/NIM and llama.cpp as benchmark-only
kept.what_to_change: Do not move Open WebUI or the Telegram bot off the vLLM OpenAI endpoint. If you want proof, run SGLang once, side by side, only for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Use lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.15-cu130 (or newer, cu130 only) with --tp 1 --mem-fraction-static <=0.75 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 --speculative-algorithm NEXTN --speculative-num-steps 3 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4. Do not try TRT-LLM or NIM for these models: the Spark TRT-LLM playbook (release:1.3.0rc13) lists Nemotron, GPT-OSS, Llama, Qwen3 and Phi-4, with no Gemma 4 or Qwen3.6/3.8, and I found no NIM for them on Spark.
kept.expected_gain: No speed gain from switching. The benefit is avoiding weeks of migration and regressions in parsers, vision and MTP. On the same GB10, Qwen3.6-35B NVFP4 + MTP decodes at 92.2 tok/s on SGLang and 93.7 tok/s on vLLM at 64k, with TTFT 222 ms vs 223 ms at 1k.
evidence: Weschera/qwen-sglang-dgx-spark README (corrected 2026-07-12): SGLang v0.5.15-cu130 92.2 tok/s vs vLLM 93.7 tok/s single-stream at 64k with prefix caching off; 65.4 vs 70.9 at 256k; author withdrew an earlier 10-40x SGLang claim as a cache artifact

ai-muninn part 19 (Apr-Aug 2026): SGLang 0.5.4 and 0.5.10 crashed on Qwen3.6 NVFP4 on GB10 (kernel crash, OOM with --disable-cuda-graph); xomoxcc/dgx-spark-sglang maintainer reports cutlass_moe_fp4 device-side assert on GB10's 101 KB smem
build.nvidia.com/spark/trt-llm playbook: model matrix has no Gemma 4 / Qwen3.6; container nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc13
NVIDIA forum 379766 (2026-08-10): Gemma-4-26B-A4B+MTP vLLM 54.9 tok/s, TTFT 94 ms vs Ollama(llama.cpp) Q4 49.6 tok/s, TTFT 511 ms
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Directly applies. Our stack depends on vLLM-specific features: the Gemma 4 MTP drafter (vLLM >=0.21), the qwen3/qwen3_xml/gemma4 parsers, vision, and prefix caching shared by Open WebUI and the Telegram agent loop. No alternative engine is faster on GB10 for these models, so migration effort (days to weeks) brings no latency benefit.
kept.risk: Low if we stay. If the SGLang A/B is attempted: about 6-minute startup, unified-memory exhaustion can hang the node and need a power cycle (keep mem-fraction <=0.8, chunked prefill around 8k), and the second engine needs memory we don't have (~15 GiB free). Stop the Qwen3.6 vLLM instance first.
kept.test_plan: Optional. Stop the vLLM Qwen3.6 instance, start SGLang with the command above, and run llama-benchy (or the vLLM bench serve client) against both with prefix caching disabled: pp 1k/8k, tg 256, concurrency 1, 5 runs each. Accept SGLang only if it is >=15% faster on both TTFT and decode and passes 20 Uzbek tool-call prompts. Otherwise delete it.
kept.verifier_reason: The conclusion holds. The numbers it cites show SGLang roughly equal to vLLM, slightly slower at 256k. SGLang has reported GB10 crashes (cutlass_moe_fp4 smem assert, OOM), and the TRT-LLM Spark matrix does not cover Gemma 4 or Qwen3.6/3.8. Our stack depends on vLLM-only pieces: the Gemma 4 MTP drafter, the gemma4/qwen3 parsers, vision, and prefix caching shared by Open WebUI and the Telegram bot. The optional SGLang A/B is weak, though. With about 15 GiB free, a second engine only fits if a vLLM instance is stopped, and a hung unified-memory node needs a power cycle. The expected result is no better than +-2%, so it fails its own >=15% acceptance bar before it starts. That makes the A/B a poor use of time.
kept.corrected_change: Keep vLLM 0.31 as the only engine. Drop the SGLang A/B from the plan. Revisit only if a published GB10 benchmark shows >=15% single-stream gain on Gemma-4-26B-A4B or Qwen3.8-27B with working tool and vision parsers. kept.title: Fix the unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 tokenizer truncation bug (silent 2048-token cutoff)
kept.what_to_change: Inside the vLLM container, check the HF cache: python -c "import json;print(json.load(open('<snapshot>/tokenizer.json'))['truncation'])". If it shows max_length 2048 (or 16384 for unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4), re-pull the fixed unsloth revision. As a stopgap, bind-mount a copy of unsloth's own tokenizer.json with only "truncation": null, read-only, over the snapshot path. Do not copy the file from Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B, since other fields differ. Pin the model revision in the serve command (--revision <sha>).
kept.expected_gain: Correctness rather than speed, and possibly the biggest 'smartness' win for the Pro model. Without the fix, every prompt over 2048 tokens is silently truncated. That covers system prompt + tool schemas + RAG chunks + memory, which in Open WebUI with native tools easily exceeds 2k. Images over ~1.4 MP also fail with a placeholder-count ValueError.
evidence: NVIDIA forum thread 380244 'Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 on a single DGX Spark ... a tokenizer bug worth knowing about': unsloth tokenizer.json shipped truncation max_length 2048; text silently cut, 1920x1200 image -> 2280 visual tokens cut to 2048; unsloth has since uploaded a fix; unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4 still has max_length 16384
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies if our Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 is the unsloth checkpoint (the most common NVFP4 build). Our Open WebUI tool schemas, bge-m3 RAG context and memory injection mean most real requests exceed 2048 tokens. A truncated system prompt or tool list would show up exactly as the 'not smart / misses tools' complaint.
kept.risk: Very low: a config/file-level change and a model restart. Pinning a revision prevents silent upstream changes.
kept.test_plan: Send a 6k-token prompt with a unique fact at the start and a question at the end. Before the fix the model can't answer; after the fix it can. Check that usage.prompt_tokens in the response equals the true count (not 2048). Send a 1920x1200 screenshot to the screenshot->Excel tool and confirm no ValueError.
kept.verifier_reason: This is cheap to check, risks almost nothing, and is high-impact if it applies. One caveat: transformers' PreTrainedTokenizerFast normally calls no_truncation() when truncation=False, so text truncation may not reproduce on every path. The multimodal processor path is the more likely one to hit it. That makes the diagnostic the important part: compare usage.prompt_tokens against the real count. It only applies if our checkpoint really is unsloth's. Pinning the revision is good practice either way.
kept.corrected_change: First verify: send a ~6k-token prompt and check that usage.prompt_tokens is ~6000, not 2048. Also inspect tokenizer.json 'truncation' in the HF snapshot. Only if it is truncated: re-download just tokenizer.json from the fixed unsloth revision with hf download --revision <sha> (a few MB, not the weights), restart, and pin --revision <sha> in the serve command. Use a read-only bind-mount of unsloth's own tokenizer.json with "truncation": null only as a stopgap. Do this before any Qwen3.8 benchmarking.

kept.title: Retune Gemma-4-26B-A4B MTP: sweep num_speculative_tokens 2/3/4 with the official -it assistant drafter, and A/B the FP8-Dynamic target
kept.what_to_change: Keep vLLM 0.31. Serve nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 with --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","model":"google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-assistant","num_speculative_tokens":N}' and --kv-cache-dtype fp8. Sweep N=2,3,4 on real Uzbek chat and tool prompts. Separately A/B the target RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-Dynamic with the same drafter at N=4, but only if memory allows: about +10 GB (≈27 GB vs 16.5 GB of weights), so it probably needs a lower --max-model-len or the Qwen3.6 instance kept offline. Confirm in the startup log that the MoE/linear backend is a real kernel (Marlin/FlashInfer CUTLASS/b12x), never an emulation fallback.
kept.expected_gain: Today we get ~50 tok/s. Published single-stream on GB10: NVFP4-it + MTP γ=4 = 76.9 tok/s, FP8-Dynamic-it + MTP γ=4 = 108.8 tok/s (2.66x). An independent user reproduced only ~75-80 tok/s with FP8 in a production config. A realistic target is 65-80 tok/s, i.e. +30-60% decode, with no change to TTFT (~94 ms).
evidence: ai-muninn part 27 (updated Jul 2026): NVIDIA NVFP4-it baseline 30.23 -> 76.88 tok/s at γ=4; RedHat FP8-it 40.85 -> 74.51 (γ=2) / 108.78 (γ=4); drafter google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-assistant (~870 MB BF16); a base (non -it) target with the drafter slowed to 25 tok/s; MTP in stock vLLM since v0.21.0 (PR #41745)

NVIDIA forum 379766: NVFP4 + MTP n=2 = 54.9 tok/s and the author found 2 beat 4 (acceptance 0.84 -> 0.27 by position). This conflicts with the above, so a sweep on our own prompts is needed; Uzbek text may have lower acceptance than English
Reddit snapshot May 2026: FP8-Dynamic + assistant drafter, 4 spec tokens: ~80 tok/s minimal config, ~75 tok/s production feature set; could not reproduce 108
Same forum post: NVFP4 emulation fallback = ~1.1 tok/s vs 77.1 with FlashInfer CUTLASS kernels
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Directly applies to the default Gemma model in Open WebUI and the Telegram bot. Acceptance rate on Uzbek may differ from English benchmarks, which is why the sweep must use our own prompts. The thinking budget of 512 tokens is decode-bound, so higher tok/s shortens time-to-answer almost linearly.
kept.risk: Medium-low. FP8 adds ~10 GB, and we only have ~15 GiB free, so OOM or reduced KV/context is likely unless another model is unloaded. MTP output is not byte-deterministic. Check that the gemma4 tool-call/reasoning parsers still behave with MTP enabled (streamed tool-call JSON).
kept.test_plan: Use llama-benchy or vllm bench serve with concurrency 1, prefix caching off, 30 real Uzbek prompts (10 chat, 10 tool-call, 10 vision), tg 512. Record tok/s, TTFT and spec acceptance from /metrics (vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens / num_draft_tokens) for N=2,3,4 on NVFP4, then FP8 at N=4. Keep the fastest config that passes 20/20 tool-call parses and has unchanged answer quality on a 20-question Uzbek eval.
kept.verifier_reason: The N sweep on our own Uzbek prompts is low-risk and worth doing. Sources disagree on whether N=2 or N=4 is better (acceptance by position 0.84 -> 0.27 in one report), and our ~50 tok/s already matches the published n=2 figure (54.9), so the cheap sweep is the useful part. The claimed 65-80 tok/s target is optimistic. The 108 tok/s FP8 number was not reproduced (75-80 in production configs), and Uzbek acceptance is likely lower than English. The FP8 A/B costs ~+10 GB against ~15 GiB free, which is unsafe on a unified-memory node that can hang while the Qwen3.8 Pro instance is resident. Before running anything, confirm the drafter repo name and the speculative-config key spelling in vLLM 0.31's docs.
kept.corrected_change: Step 1, safe: on the current nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 target, sweep num_speculative_tokens 2/3/4 (and 1) with the -it assistant drafter you already use. Check the drafter id and config keys against vLLM 0.31 docs. Use 30 real Uzbek prompts (chat, tool-call, vision) and read acceptance from /metrics. Keep the best N that passes 20/20 tool-call parses. Confirm the startup log shows a real NVFP4 MoE kernel (Marlin/FlashInfer CUTLASS), not emulation. Step 2, only with the Qwen3.8 instance stopped (a maintenance-window test): A/B the RedHatAI FP8-Dynamic target at the best N. Adopt FP8 only if it is >=20% faster and the combined memory plan still leaves >=8 GiB free. Realistic expectation: +10-40% decode, not +60%.

kept.title: Speed up the Pro model (Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4) with MTP n=3, fp8 KV and the Triton attention backend
kept.what_to_change: Change the Qwen3.8-27B vLLM serve flags to: --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN (FlashAttention can't do fp8 KV on sm_121), --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-prefix-caching --reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml (or qwen3_coder; test both) --enable-auto-tool-choice. Sweep num_speculative_tokens 3/5. If stock 0.31 underperforms, try the community GB10 image eugr/spark-vllm-b12x (nightly) as an A/B only.
kept.expected_gain: Our ~25 tok/s matches the forum's MTP-5 result (24.7). Reported GB10 single-node recipes with MTP-3 + fp8 KV + triton_attn reach 39-45 tok/s, i.e. +50-80%. Other users on the same recipe saw only 18-31 tok/s, so treat ~30-35 tok/s as the realistic expectation. fp8 KV also roughly halves KV memory, which helps our 15 GiB budget.
evidence: NVIDIA forum 380244: unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4, vLLM 0.26.1rc1 nightly: MTP off 11.4 tok/s, n=3 23.6, n=5 24.7, n=8 21.7; TTFT 0.40 s on a 64-token prompt; prefill 1734 tok/s at 4.5k, 853 tok/s at 48k; parsers qwen3 / qwen3_xml

Same thread, styles01 recipe: 39 tok/s decode with MTP n=3, --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder, image ghcr.io/drowzeys/keys-vllm-027-gb10-qwen38:mtp3-20260813; others measured 26 (31 peak), 15-25, 18.3 tok/s

contextstudios recipe from github.com/Weschera/Qwen3.8-27B-DGX-Spark-Quant-Ladder (Sep 29 2026): 45 tok/s single request, NVFP4 unsloth + fp8 KV + triton_attn + MTP; notes FA can't do fp8 KV on sm_121
forum 380258: Unsloth NVFP4 output throughput 30-34% higher than official FP8 at 16 concurrent (no MTP)
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies to the Pro tier. It is a dense 27B, so decode is bandwidth-bound (~14 GB of weights per token at 273 GB/s), and MTP is the only lever that meaningfully raises single-stream speed. No engine switch changes that ceiling.
kept.risk: Medium. Results vary widely between users (18-45 tok/s), and the gain may be smaller on Uzbek. fp8 KV can slightly degrade long-context accuracy. Community images are unofficial, so pin by digest. Requires the tokenizer fix (recommendation 1) first, or benchmarks are invalid.
kept.test_plan: After the tokenizer fix, A/B the current flags vs new flags: concurrency 1, prefix cache off, prompts at depth 0 / 8k / 32k, tg 512, 5 runs each. Measure decode tok/s, TTFT and acceptance rate. Run 20 Uzbek multi-step tool tasks (SearXNG + fetch + SQL) and require equal or better success. Roll back if decode at 32k drops below the current setup.
kept.verifier_reason: The direction is plausible. For a dense 27B NVFP4 (~14-16 GB of weights at 273 GB/s), the ceiling is about 18 tok/s without speculation, so MTP plus a cheaper KV cache are the only real levers. Our 25 tok/s already looks like MTP is on, so the gain from moving n=5 to n=3 is small; the forum data shows 23.6 vs 24.7. The 39-45 tok/s claims are outliers, and others measured 15-31, so +20-40% is a realistic range. fp8 KV is a real memory win. The claim that FlashAttention can't do fp8 KV on sm_121 comes from community reports, so check it against vLLM 0.31's startup log. The community images (drowzeys/eugr) are unofficial third-party containers with a supply-chain risk. --enable-chunked-prefill is already the default.
kept.corrected_change: After the tokenizer check, change only stock vLLM 0.31 flags: --kv-cache-dtype fp8, plus --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN if the log shows FlashAttention rejecting fp8 KV. Also --max-num-batched-tokens 8192, --enable-prefix-caching, --reasoning-parser qwen3, and --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml vs qwen3_coder (A/B). Then sweep MTP num_speculative_tokens 2/3/4/5. Do not use unofficial community images in production. If one is ever tested, pin it by digest, run it offline as an A/B only, and never point the bot at it. Target 28-35 tok/s. Require equal Uzbek multi-step tool success, and check 32k-context answer quality with fp8 KV before adopting.

kept.title: Run the reranker (and embedder) on the GPU through small vLLM pooling servers, and use Open WebUI's external reranker and OpenAI embedding engines
kept.what_to_change: Run two small vLLM processes next to the LLMs, using the same sm_121 vLLM 0.31 build that already works. (1) Embedder: `vllm serve BAAI/bge-m3 --runner pooling --port 8010 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.03 --max-model-len 8192 --served-model-name bge-m3`. (2) Reranker: `vllm serve BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --runner pooling --port 8011 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.03 --max-model-len 1024 --served-model-name bge-reranker-v2-m3`. vLLM's scoring docs list it as XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification, so it needs no overrides. Then set these in Open WebUI: RAG_EMBEDDING_ENGINE=openai, RAG_OPENAI_API_BASE_URL=http://<host>:8010/v1, RAG_EMBEDDING_MODEL=bge-m3, RAG_EMBEDDING_BATCH_SIZE=32, RAG_RERANKING_ENGINE=external, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_URL=http://<host>:8011/v1/rerank (it must include the full path, because nothing is appended), RAG_RERANKING_MODEL=bge-reranker-v2-m3, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_TIMEOUT=10. Keep the same bge-m3 model so no re-indexing is needed; only the runtime moves. If you switch the vector source, re-index once to be safe.
kept.expected_gain: This is my estimate, not something I measured on GB10. On the CPU path (the default non-:cuda image on aarch64), reranking about 20 chunks of 400-500 tokens with a 568M XLM-R cross-encoder usually takes several seconds. On the GPU it should take roughly 50-200 ms. Query embedding drops to tens of ms. It also takes the torch/sentence-transformers models out of the Open WebUI process, which lowers its RAM use and makes startup faster.
evidence: vLLM scoring docs list BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 (XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification) as supported and expose Cohere-compatible /v1/rerank: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/pooling_models/scoring/
vLLM pooling docs: --runner pooling, /v1/embeddings, /v1/rerank endpoints: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/pooling_models/

Open WebUI env reference: RAG_RERANKING_ENGINE=external, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_URL must include /v1/rerank, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_TIMEOUT, RAG_RERANKING_BATCH_SIZE default 32, RAG_EMBEDDING_BATCH_SIZE default 1: https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/env-configuration/

Open WebUI issue #19900: the external reranker used to block the whole event loop (sync requests.post). A fix landed in dev in Dec 2025, so 0.12 should include it: https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui/issues/19900
I found no published arm64 :cuda Open WebUI image (NVIDIA's Spark playbook uses :ollama), so the local reranker most likely runs on CPU today: https://build.nvidia.com/spark/open-webui
kept.applies_to_our_stack: This fits the stack directly. vLLM already runs on sm_121, both models are about 0.57B params (around 1.2 GB bf16 each), and GPU memory comes from the same unified pool. Budget is about 2x(1.2 GB weights + ~1-2 GB CUDA context/activations), roughly 5-6 GB in total. That fits in the ~15 GiB free if --gpu-memory-utilization stays at 0.03 (about 3.8 GB each on a 128 GB pool). Lower it to 0.02 if KV-cache allocation complains. The Telegram bot can call the same :8010/:8011 endpoints for its own RAG.
kept.risk: Low to medium. vLLM pooling on sm_121 might need the same custom build flags as your LLM build. Each extra process adds CUDA context overhead (about 0.5-1 GB) and competes a little with LLM decode bandwidth during reranking, but only for about 100 ms. If memory is too tight, run only the reranker on vLLM and leave the embedder local, because query-time embedding of one short query is cheap even on CPU (Arm's DGX Spark RAG blog argues CPU is fine for small-batch embedding).
kept.test_plan: 1) `curl :8011/v1/rerank -d '{"model":"bge-reranker-v2-m3","query":"Soliq imtiyozlari kimga beriladi?","documents":[...20 Uzbek chunks...]}'`, then time it with `time` and check that the scores match sentence-transformers CrossEncoder output within about 1e-3. 2) In Open WebUI, ask the same 20 Uzbek questions against one knowledge base before and after the change, and log time-to-first-token with the browser network tab or OWUI logs (DEBUG on RAG). 3) Run `nvidia-smi`/`free -g` during load and confirm the LLMs keep at least 5 GB headroom.
kept.verifier_reason: The mechanics check out. vLLM lists bge-reranker-v2-m3 (XLMRobertaForSequenceClassification) and bge-m3 as pooling models with Cohere-style /v1/rerank and /v1/embeddings. I confirmed in the OWUI docs that RAG_RERANKING_ENGINE=external is valid, that RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_URL needs the full /v1/rerank path, and that RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_TIMEOUT and RAG_EMBEDDING_BATCH_SIZE (default 1) exist. Moving cross-encoder reranking off the Grace CPU is the most plausible TTFT win for one user. The memory math is optimistic, though. Each vLLM process carries roughly 1-2 GB of host-side Python/torch RSS on top of its GPU slice, and on unified memory the two are the same pool. Two processes with CUDA graphs are more like 7-9 GB of the ~15 GiB free. Also, --gpu-memory-utilization is a fraction of the total 128 GB and vLLM checks it against currently free memory at startup, so starting order matters. Moving the embedder gains little because query embedding is already cheap on CPU. The scores should agree because CrossEncoder applies sigmoid for num_labels=1, and so does vLLM's score output.
kept.corrected_change: Phase 1, reranker only: `vllm serve BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 --runner pooling --port 8011 --served-model-name bge-reranker-v2-m3 --max-model-len 1024 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.03 --enforce-eager`. Start it after both LLMs are up. --enforce-eager skips CUDA-graph capture memory and startup time. Then set RAG_RERANKING_ENGINE=external, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_URL=http://<host>:8011/v1/rerank, RAG_RERANKING_MODEL=bge-reranker-v2-m3, RAG_EXTERNAL_RERANKER_TIMEOUT=10. Measure the real footprint with `free -g` and the process RSS. Expect about 3-4 GB. Phase 2, only if at least 6 GB is still free and indexing or bulk embedding is slow: add the bge-m3 embedder the same way (--max-model-len 8192 --enforce-eager), with RAG_EMBEDDING_ENGINE=openai, RAG_OPENAI_API_BASE_URL=http://<host>:8010/v1, RAG_EMBEDDING_MODEL=bge-m3, RAG_EMBEDDING_BATCH_SIZE=32. Compare cosine against the existing SentenceTransformer vectors on 20 chunks (expect >0.999) before trusting that no re-index is needed. Add both processes to systemd with restart, and make the Telegram bot call the same endpoints.

kept.title: Build a 50-100 question Uzbek retrieval eval set before swapping models, then A/B bge-m3 against Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and bge-reranker-v2-m3 against Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B
kept.what_to_change: Write a small script (Jupyter is fine) that takes 50-100 real Uzbek questions with a gold chunk ID each, from your own documents and in both Latin and Cyrillic script. Run each candidate through the vLLM endpoints and measure Recall@20 after first-stage retrieval and nDCG@5/MRR after reranking. Candidates: embedders BAAI/bge-m3 (baseline) and Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B --runner pooling`, with the instruction prefix on queries set through RAG_EMBEDDING_QUERY_PREFIX, e.g. 'Instruct: Given a question, retrieve relevant passages\nQuery: '). Rerankers BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 (baseline) and Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (`vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B --runner pooling --hf_overrides '{"architectures":["Qwen3ForSequenceClassification"],"classifier_from_token":["no","yes"],"is_original_qwen3_reranker":true}'`, which needs the qwen3_reranker.jinja score template). Swap only if a candidate wins by at least 3-5 points on your own set.
kept.expected_gain: Unknown in advance. I found no public benchmark with Uzbek retrieval scores for any of these models. The best multilingual-retrieval proxy (MIRACL) actually favours the current bge-reranker-v2-m3 (69.3) over Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (57.7) and jina-reranker-v3 (66.8). So the likely result is to keep the bge pair and stop guessing. Qwen3-Embedding-8B tops MMTEB overall but is too large and slow for our memory budget.
evidence: Jina's comparison table (vendor-reported): bge-reranker-v2-m3 BEIR 56.51 / MIRACL 69.32; Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B BEIR 56.28 / MIRACL 57.70; jina-reranker-v3 MIRACL 66.83: https://jina.ai/news/jina-reranker-v3-0-6b-listwise-reranker-for-sota-multilingual-retrieval/
jina-reranker-v3.5 (Jul/Aug 2026) is CC-BY-NC-4.0, so it is non-commercial only: https://jina.ai/models/jina-reranker-v3.5/
Qwen3-Embedding model card and paper (100+ languages, 8B was MMTEB #1 in Jun 2025): https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B , https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05176
vLLM Qwen3-Reranker hf_overrides and score templates: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/pooling_models/scoring/
My searches found no Uzbek-specific embedding/retrieval benchmark (honest gap).
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Every candidate is 0.6B or smaller, so each fits the same ~3-4 GB slot as recommendation 1. The eval set doubles as a regression test whenever chunking or hybrid settings change.
kept.risk: Low. Changing the embedder means re-embedding every knowledge base (Admin > Documents > Reindex), and mixing vectors from two embedders silently breaks retrieval. Qwen3-Reranker's original checkpoint depends on the yes/no template, and if the template is missing the scores look plausible but are wrong. Check that vLLM applies the template by comparing against the HF reference snippet on 5 pairs.
kept.test_plan: Use one script with a fixed eval set and report Recall@5/20, MRR@10, and p50/p95 latency per model for 20-candidate reranks. Accept a change only if quality improves by at least 3 points and p95 latency stays at or below 300 ms.
kept.verifier_reason: This is sound and honest. The models exist, the Qwen3-Reranker hf_overrides (Qwen3ForSequenceClassification, classifier_from_token [no,yes], is_original_qwen3_reranker) match the vLLM docs, RAG_EMBEDDING_QUERY_PREFIX exists in OWUI, and every candidate fits the memory budget. The weak points are as follows. With 50-100 questions a 3-5 point gap is close to noise, so a significance check is needed. The MIRACL numbers are Jina vendor-reported. Putting a literal newline inside an env-var prefix is fragile in docker/compose. Running a second embedder or reranker at the same time as recommendation 1's servers adds 3-4 GB, so candidates must be tested one at a time.
kept.corrected_change: Same plan, with these changes. Use 100 or more questions if possible: Latin and Cyrillic, plus a few with apostrophe variants. Gemma can draft question/gold-chunk pairs from your own documents, which you then check by hand. Report bootstrap 95% CIs or a paired test, and switch only if the CI excludes 0 and the gain is at least 3 points. Run candidates sequentially: stop the baseline vLLM pooling server before starting a candidate, and don't keep both resident. Set the Qwen3-Embedding query prefix through the Admin UI or a properly quoted .env value, and check that the newline survives by logging one embedded query. For Qwen3-Reranker, check vLLM scores against the HF reference on 5 pairs, as proposed. The default expectation is to keep the bge pair.

kept.title: Tune hybrid search for Uzbek: enable it, lower the BM25 weight, normalise apostrophes and script before indexing, and widen the candidate pool
kept.what_to_change: Settings: ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH=true, RAG_HYBRID_BM25_WEIGHT=0.3 (start here; Uzbek is agglutinative and OWUI's BM25 has no Uzbek stemmer, so surface-form matching misses inflections like 'soliq/soliqlar/soliqqa'), RAG_TOP_K=20 (candidates into the reranker), RAG_TOP_K_RERANKER=5, RAG_RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD=0.0 at first (raise to about 0.05-0.1 only after you look at score distributions), ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH_ENRICHED_TEXTS=true (filenames and section titles help keyword hits). Normalise text before upload, either as a preprocessing step in the ingestion path or as an OWUI filter function on queries: map the apostrophe variants ‘ ’ ʻ ʼ ` ' to a single form so that o‘/g‘ and the tutuq belgisi are consistent, and add a Cyrillic-to-Latin transliteration copy for Cyrillic documents. Do the same transliteration on queries, so BM25 matches across scripts. Dense bge-m3 is partly script-robust, but BM25 is not.
kept.expected_gain: Better recall on names, numbers, law/article codes and exact terms where dense retrieval is weak. Apostrophe normalisation alone can fix a whole class of BM25 misses ('o'zbek' vs 'oʻzbek' tokenise differently). Expect a few points of Recall@20 on your eval set. That is an estimate; measure it.
evidence: Open WebUI env reference: ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH (default False), RAG_HYBRID_BM25_WEIGHT default 0.5 (1=keyword only, 0=vector only), ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH_ENRICHED_TEXTS, RAG_TOP_K default 3, RAG_TOP_K_RERANKER default 3, RAG_RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD default 0.0: https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/env-configuration/
Uzbek orthography uses ʻ (U+02BB) and ʼ (U+02BC), but documents in the wild mix them with ‘ ’ ' and `. That comes from my general knowledge, not a fetched source.
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Configuration only, inside Open WebUI 0.12. The defaults (TOP_K=3, reranker top 3) are far too narrow for a reranker to help. Note that the enriched-texts option is skipped for native hybrid on Milvus 2.5+ and pgvector, per the docs.
kept.risk: Low. A higher TOP_K means more rerank pairs, which is fine on GPU but slow on CPU, so do recommendation 1 first. Transliteration is lossy for some Cyrillic letters (ц, щ, ъ), so keep the original text in the chunk shown to the LLM and use the transliterated copy only for indexing and search.
kept.test_plan: On the eval set, sweep BM25 weight over 0, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5 and TOP_K over 10, 20, 30, and report Recall@20 and nDCG@5 after reranking. Include about 10 queries written in Cyrillic against Latin docs and the reverse, plus 10 with apostrophe variants.
kept.verifier_reason: The flags exist with the stated defaults: ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH, RAG_HYBRID_BM25_WEIGHT=0.5, ENABLE_RAG_HYBRID_SEARCH_ENRICHED_TEXTS default False with the Milvus/pgvector caveat, and RAG_TOP_K and RAG_TOP_K_RERANKER both default 3. Stock OWUI cannot 'index a transliterated copy but show the original chunk to the LLM': the chunk it embeds or BM25-indexes is the chunk it returns. That needs a custom ingestion pipeline or uploading duplicate documents. Uzbek Cyrillic-to-Latin conversion is close to deterministic (the lossy direction is Latin to Cyrillic), so converting the whole corpus to Latin is the simpler choice. A query-side filter that rewrites the user message also changes what the LLM sees, which is acceptable for apostrophes and transliteration. BM25 in OWUI does little preprocessing, so punctuation and case can also cause misses. Normalisation should cover lowercasing and punctuation only if you control ingestion.

Do this only after the reranker is on the GPU. kept.title: Chunking for Uzbek: use the token splitter so chunks fit the reranker's window, with markdown headers and merging of small chunks
kept.what_to_change: Set RAG_TEXT_SPLITTER=token, CHUNK_SIZE=400, CHUNK_OVERLAP=60, ENABLE_MARKDOWN_HEADER_TEXT_SPLITTER=true, CHUNK_MIN_SIZE_TARGET=150. Run the reranker with --max-model-len 1024 (or 512 if it is still too slow). The reason: Uzbek tokenises into noticeably more XLM-R tokens per word than English, so the default CHUNK_SIZE=1000 characters (character splitter) gives uneven chunks. Fixed token-sized chunks keep query+chunk under the reranker's window, so nothing gets truncated mid-chunk. For PDFs, extract to markdown first (OWUI's Docling or Mistral-free pipelines) so the header splitter has structure to work with.
kept.expected_gain: More stable reranker scores, because truncation no longer hides the relevant tail. Fewer, denser chunks also mean fewer rerank pairs and less context fed to Gemma or Qwen, which cuts prefill time for the 50 tok/s model. Size of the gain is an estimate; check it on the eval set.
evidence: Open WebUI env reference: RAG_TEXT_SPLITTER (character|token|token_transformers), CHUNK_SIZE default 1000, CHUNK_OVERLAP default 100, CHUNK_MIN_SIZE_TARGET (requires markdown header splitter), ENABLE_MARKDOWN_HEADER_TEXT_SPLITTER default True: https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/env-configuration/
bge-m3 accepts up to 8192 tokens, but cross-encoder rerankers are typically trained and run at 512-1024. Multilingual E5 is limited to 512: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05672
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Configuration only. Existing knowledge bases need re-chunking and re-indexing for the change to apply.
kept.risk: Low. The 'token' splitter counts tiktoken tokens, not XLM-R tokens, so 400 tiktoken tokens of Uzbek may be about 500-650 XLM-R tokens. That is why the reranker max length is 1024. Verify on a sample with the bge-m3 tokenizer.
kept.test_plan: Re-index one knowledge base three ways (char 1000/100, token 400/60, token 256/40) and compare Recall@20, nDCG@5, average context tokens sent to the LLM, and TTFT on the eval set.
kept.verifier_reason: The goal is right, but the mechanism and the risk analysis are wrong. OWUI's 'token' splitter is tiktoken cl100k_base, which I confirmed in the docs. cl100k splits Uzbek into many more tokens per word than XLM-R's 250k multilingual vocab does, so 400 tiktoken tokens of Uzbek is likely around 250-350 XLM-R tokens, not the claimed 500-650. Chunks would come out smaller than intended. OWUI already has the correct option: RAG_TEXT_SPLITTER=token_transformers with RAG_TOKENIZER_MODEL, which counts real bge-m3/XLM-R tokens. It isn't available on the slim image. CHUNK_MIN_SIZE_TARGET does exist and only works with ENABLE_MARKDOWN_HEADER_TEXT_SPLITTER, as the recommendation says. The bge-reranker-v2-m3 model card examples use max_length 512, so 1024 is the ceiling, not a requirement.
kept.corrected_change: Set RAG_TEXT_SPLITTER=token_transformers, RAG_TOKENIZER_MODEL=BAAI/bge-m3 (non-slim image), CHUNK_SIZE=400, CHUNK_OVERLAP=50-60, ENABLE_MARKDOWN_HEADER_TEXT_SPLITTER=true, CHUNK_MIN_SIZE_TARGET=150. Run the reranker with --max-model-len 512-1024. 400 XLM-R chunk tokens plus the query fits in 512, which is the faster setting. If you're stuck on the slim image, use RAG_TEXT_SPLITTER=token with CHUNK_SIZE of about 550-600, measured on a sample against the bge-m3 tokenizer so chunks land near 400 XLM-R tokens. Re-index the knowledge bases and compare against char 1000/100 on the eval set, including average context tokens and TTFT.

kept.title: Cut LLM-side RAG latency: no extra query-generation call for simple chats, and the fast model for query rewriting
kept.what_to_change: Open WebUI makes an extra LLM call to generate retrieval queries before RAG (ENABLE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY_GENERATION=True by default). On a 25-50 tok/s model with thinking enabled, that call can cost more than the whole retrieval. Options: (a) set the Task Model (Admin > Settings > Interface > Task model) to the fastest model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (110-134 tok/s), with thinking disabled for tasks; (b) set ENABLE_QUERIES_CACHE=true so web search and RAG reuse the generated queries; (c) if your eval shows raw questions retrieve as well as generated ones, set ENABLE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY_GENERATION=false. For small single-document chats, try per-knowledge-base full-context mode (RAG_FULL_CONTEXT) instead of retrieval when the document is shorter than about 8-16k tokens.
kept.expected_gain: Removes one serial LLM round-trip, roughly 1-4 s per RAG turn depending on the model and thinking settings (estimate). That is likely the biggest remaining TTFT cost once reranking moves to the GPU.
evidence: Open WebUI env reference: ENABLE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY_GENERATION default True, ENABLE_QUERIES_CACHE default False, QUERY_GENERATION_PROMPT_TEMPLATE, RAG_FULL_CONTEXT, BYPASS_EMBEDDING_AND_RETRIEVAL: https://docs.openwebui.com/reference/env-configuration/
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Directly applicable. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is already downloaded, and its weaker Uzbek multi-step agent ability matters little for one-line query rewriting. If memory does not allow keeping it resident, point the task model at Gemma-4-26B-A4B with the thinking budget set to 0 for tasks.
kept.risk: Low to medium. Disabling query generation hurts multi-turn follow-ups ('what about the second one?'), because the raw last message lacks context. The query cache needs testing on 0.12. Full-context mode floods the context on large documents.
kept.test_plan: Turn on OWUI debug logging and time each stage (query-gen, embed, search, rerank, first token) for 20 eval questions under three configs: default; task model = A3B with no thinking; query-gen off. Compare TTFT p50/p95 and answer correctness, with you grading the answers.
kept.verifier_reason: The flags exist (ENABLE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY_GENERATION default True, ENABLE_QUERIES_CACHE, RAG_FULL_CONTEXT), and a serial query-generation call with thinking enabled is a real TTFT cost for one user. But the main option, making Qwen3.6-35B-A3B the task model, is not applicable. It is not resident, and its NVFP4 weights (~20 GB plus KV) do not fit in ~15 GiB free alongside Gemma and Qwen 27B. The fallback should be the main plan. ENABLE_QUERIES_CACHE only reuses web-search queries for KB retrieval within the same request, so its gain is small and situational. RAG_FULL_CONTEXT is global; per-file full-document use is the UI toggle on attached files.
kept.corrected_change: Set the Task Model to the already-resident Gemma-4-26B-A4B (~50 tok/s), using a workspace model preset with thinking disabled for tasks (no reasoning budget / enable_thinking=false via chat_template_kwargs). Keep query generation on by default because it matters for multi-turn follow-ups, and turn it off only if the eval shows raw queries retrieve as well. Shorten QUERY_GENERATION_PROMPT_TEMPLATE to ask for 1-2 queries in Uzbek. Enable ENABLE_QUERIES_CACHE as a low-risk extra. For small single documents, use the per-file 'entire document' mode instead of global RAG_FULL_CONTEXT. Consider A3B as a task model only if you ever free enough memory to keep it resident.

kept.title: Keep the injected memory block stable across turns so vLLM's prefix cache keeps hitting (store only 'user' memories, or turn off auto-injection)
kept.what_to_change: How Open WebUI v0.12.0 builds the memory block (backend/open_webui/utils/memory.py, add_memory_context): it takes ALL memories of type `user`, sorted in a stable order (stable since v0.11.1, #28292). It then adds a 'Memory Neighborhood' plus a 'Relevant Context' section, which is the top-8 vector hits (k=8) for `context`-type memories, queried with bge-m3 against the last 7 user messages. The whole block is APPENDED TO THE END of the system message on every request. Every time the retrieved `context` hits change, the system message changes, and vLLM has to prefill the entire conversation history again, including large tool results from page fetches and the browser. Pick one option. (A) Recommended: keep personalization in `user`-type memories only. Delete or convert existing `context` memories in Settings > Personalization > Memory, and leave background review off or watch what it writes. The block then changes only when a memory actually changes. (B) Set ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT=false (Admin > General > 'Memory System Context') and paste a hand-curated profile of 1200 characters or less into the model's static system prompt (Workspace > Models > Sarob > System Prompt). Keep the memory tools (search_memories, add_memory, etc.) for on-demand recall, and add one line to the system prompt: 'Foydalanuvchi haqida eski ma'lumot kerak bo'lsa search_memories dan foydalan.' ('If you need older information about the user, use search_memories.') Option B also skips the per-turn bge-m3 query embedding. Either way, keep volatile things out of the system prompt: no {{CURRENT_DATETIME}} or {{CURRENT_TIME}} there (CURRENT_DATE is fine, since it changes daily). Turn off File Context and Citations per the Open WebUI prompt-caching guide.
kept.expected_gain: No change in quality. Follow-up turns in long agentic chats (10-40k tokens of history with tool outputs) stop re-prefilling the whole history. On GB10, prefill for the 26B-A4B NVFP4 model is probably a few thousand tokens per second (not measured here), so this could save roughly 2-10 s of time-to-first-token per turn in long chats. Short chats see little change.
evidence: Open WebUI v0.12.0 source, utils/memory.py add_memory_context: query_memory(... k=8) over the last 7 user messages; `user` memories sorted stably; result goes into add_or_update_system_message(memory_context, messages, append=True); limits use a floor of max(250, ...)

docs.openwebui.com/features/chat-conversations/prompt-caching: memory injection is listed as high impact on the cache; it 'is retrieved against your recent messages each turn'; the mitigation given is ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT=false plus tools on demand
Release v0.11.1 notes: 'memories handed to the model now appear in a stable order ... servers that reuse their work between turns no longer reprocess the whole conversation' (#28292)
docs env-configuration: ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT default True; MEMORIES_USER_CHAR_LIMIT and MEMORIES_CONTEXT_CHAR_LIMIT default 2000
kept.applies_to_our_stack: This applies directly. Open WebUI 0.12 plus vLLM 0.31 with automatic prefix caching, which is on by default in V1. One user with long tool-heavy chats is exactly the case where cache misses hurt most. Not verified: whether prefix caching hits fully for Gemma-4's hybrid sliding-window attention with MTP enabled on this vLLM build. Check that first using the test plan.
kept.risk: Low. Option B loses automatic recall of `context` facts unless the model calls search_memories. Gemma-4-26B-A4B is not on Open WebUI's list of 'verified minimum' memory models (that list includes Qwen 3.6 27B), so on-demand recall may be inconsistent. The main risk is that the profile goes stale if it is maintained by hand.
kept.test_plan: 1) Start vLLM with --enable-prompt-tokens-details. 2) In a 15-turn chat that uses page-fetch tools, log usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens per request (from vLLM logs, or curl the same messages) and scrape /metrics for vllm:prefix_cache_hits and vllm:prefix_cache_queries. 3) Compare the current config with option A and with option B on the same scripted chat. Success means the cached/prompt ratio is at least 0.8 on turns 3 and later, and TTFT on turn 10 is lower. 4) Recall check: 10 Uzbek questions that need profile facts. Score must not drop.
kept.verifier_reason: The current open-webui main utils/memory.py confirms how the block is built. It walks the last 7 user messages, capped at 4000 chars, and runs query_memory with k=8. User memories are sorted by path, then updated_at, then id. A Memory Neighborhood (path hints) plus Relevant Context section is drawn from context-type memories. Each part is limited to max(250, limit) with a default of 2000, and the block is wrapped in <memory_context> and appended to the system message. The docs prompt-caching page confirms memory injection breaks the cache and lists ENABLE_MEMORY_SYSTEM_CONTEXT=false plus on-demand tools as the fix. The docs also confirm File Context and Citations do heavy cache damage. The variable is a persistent config with an Admin > General toggle. The gain is plausible for one user with long tool-heavy chats. Caveats: (a) with option A the bge-m3 query still runs every turn, but returns nothing to inject, so the cost is small; (b) any mid-chat add_memory/update_memory call to a user memory still changes the prefix; (c) whether prefix caching hits on Gemma-4's hybrid sliding-window attention plus MTP on this vLLM build is unverified and must be measured first.
kept.corrected_change: Same change, with these additions. With option A, also tell the model in the system prompt not to save memories mid-task; any user-memory write still invalidates the whole prefix. Option A removes both the Memory Neighborhood and Relevant Context sections, because both draw only from context-type memories. Measure first: if vLLM reports cached_tokens of about 0 even on identical consecutive requests for Gemma-4 (hybrid SWA plus MTP), this change gains nothing on that model until prefix caching works there. In that case, test it on Qwen3.8-27B as well.

kept.title: Turn on background memory review with care: it runs on the CHAT model (not the task model), and the env var is ignored after the first start
kept.what_to_change: In v0.12.0, review_memory_after_turn launches an asyncio task every MEMORIES_REVIEW_INTERVAL_TURNS user turns, and only after the reply and title/tag generation are done. It sends one non-streaming call to `model.get('id')`, which is the chat's own model, with up to 80 existing memories and the last 16 messages (each truncated to about 1.4k chars). It does not block the reply, but it does compete for the GPU with your next message. Steps: (1) Use Gemma-4-26B-A4B as the everyday model. Turn the per-model memory capability OFF for Qwen3.8-27B Pro (Workspace > Models > edit > Capabilities > Memory, the per-model switch added in v0.11.0), so reviews never run on the slow dense model. (2) Enable review through the config API, because ENABLE_MEMORY_BACKGROUND_REVIEW and MEMORIES_REVIEW_INTERVAL_TURNS have no UI toggle and the stored value overrides env after the first start. Export the current config: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/configs/export > cfg.json. Set memories.background_review.enable=true and memories.review_interval_turns=8, then POST it back to /api/v1/configs/import. (3) Because the review's JSON prompt is in English, add to the profile/system prompt: 'Xotiralarni o'zbek tilida, qisqa, bitta fakt = bitta qator yoz.' (Write memories in Uzbek, briefly, one fact per line.) (4) Review Settings > Personalization > Memory weekly. The review can add `context` memories, which undoes recommendation 1A. Either remove them or accept the cache cost.
kept.expected_gain: The assistant learns preferences and personal facts automatically without the user saying 'remember this'. That is what makes it feel more like a frontier assistant. With an interval of 8, about one extra background call per 8 turns, mostly prefill of 3-6k tokens. No added latency on the turn that triggers it.

Release v0.11.4: 'background review ... no longer runs when memories are switched off' (wording says task-model call, but the code uses the chat model id, so treat the code as authoritative)
Release v0.11.0: 'Memory as a per-model capability'
kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies to the Open WebUI 0.12 side. On a single Spark the review call batches with the user's next request in vLLM, so decode speed dips briefly rather than stalling. If Gemma's thinking budget (512) applies to this call, the reviewer may spend tokens on thinking. The code falls back to reasoning_content when parsing, so it still works.
kept.risk: Medium. The model can write wrong or duplicate memories, or save something sensitive (the prompt forbids secrets, but small models slip). Since `user` memories are always injected, a bad memory affects every chat until someone deletes it. Gemma-4-26B is not verified by Open WebUI for this task. The extra GPU load is minor.
kept.test_plan: Run 30 scripted Uzbek turns containing 5 planted durable facts (job, city, preferred currency format, child's name, preferred answer length) and 5 transient ones (lunch, mood). After the run, check the memory list. Target: at least 4/5 durable facts saved, at most 1 transient fact saved, no duplicates, written in Uzbek. Also measure TTFT of the turn right after a review fires against a turn with no review (expect under 1 s difference).
kept.verifier_reason: Confirmed in source. review_memory_after_turn runs under asyncio.create_task. model_id = model.get('id'), falling back to form_data['model']. It uses existing_memories[:80] and messages[-16:]; messages longer than 1600 chars become the first 1000 plus the last 400. It runs only when user_turns % interval == 0. Config keys are memories.background_review.enable and memories.review_interval_turns, with ENABLE_MEMORY_BACKGROUND_REVIEW default False and MEMORIES_REVIEW_INTERVAL_TURNS default 10 in config.py. Two parts are wrong or overstated. (1) Step 3: adding an Uzbek instruction to the chat system prompt probably does not reach the reviewer. The reviewer builds its own prompt from existing memories plus the last 16 messages, so the language of the saved memories is set by that internal prompt and the conversation, not by the chat system prompt. (2) Step 1: turning off the per-model Memory capability on Qwen Pro also turns off memory injection and the memory tools for that model, not only the review, so Pro chats lose personalization. The review call also inherits Gemma's thinking budget, and no chat_template_kwargs override is passed, so it costs up to 512 extra decode tokens per review (about 10 s of GPU time, in the background). Acceptable at interval 8.
kept.corrected_change: Enable through POST /api/v1/configs/import with memories.background_review.enable=true and memories.review_interval_turns=8. Export first and keep the backup, because import writes the stored config. Drop the claim that a system-prompt line controls the reviewer's language. Instead, check in the test whether memories come out in Uzbek. If not, either accept English memories (the model reads them fine) or patch the review prompt in utils/memory.py locally. Either keep memory ON for Qwen Pro and accept that reviews run on the slow model there, or turn it off knowing that also removes memory injection and the memory tools for Pro. Expect up to 512 thinking tokens per review on Gemma. Review the memory list weekly and delete context-type memories the reviewer adds if you follow recommendation 1A.

kept.title: Telegram bot: a cache-friendly compact profile in the system prompt, shared with Open WebUI's memory store, plus asynchronous post-turn extraction
kept.what_to_change: Build the bot's prompt in this order: [static persona + rules] -> [USER PROFILE block, at most about 1200 chars] -> [fixed tool schemas] -> history -> current user message. Put anything that changes per turn (current date/time, per-query recalled snippets, CBU rates) at the END, inside the latest user message, never in the system message. Get the profile from Open WebUI so both front ends share one memory: GET /api/v1/memories/ with a Bearer API key for the single user. Filter to type=='user', sort by (path, updated_at, id) exactly as Open WebUI does, render as '- path: content' lines, and cache it in-process. Rebuild only when the max updated_at changes, checked at most once per minute or on /profile. After each reply has been SENT to Telegram, run extraction in the background with asyncio.create_task (python-telegram-bot handlers can do this, or use application.create_task) every 6-8 user turns. Use the same JSON operations schema as Open WebUI (add/replace/remove, type user|context) on the last 12 messages plus the current profile. Call the Gemma-4-26B-A4B endpoint with thinking off (for example extra_body={'chat_template_kwargs': {'enable_thinking': False}}; check the exact switch in the Gemma-4 chat template on your vLLM build), temperature 0, max_tokens 400. Write results through POST /api/v1/memories/update (batch operations) or /api/v1/memories/add. Add explicit commands /eslab_qol <fakt> (remember this), /unut <id> (forget), and /profil (show profile) so the user stays in control.
kept.expected_gain: The bot and the web UI share the same personalization, so a fact learned in one shows up in the other. TTFT stays low: the system prefix is byte-identical between turns and across chats until the profile changes, so vLLM reuses the whole prefix including the tool schemas. Extraction never adds to perceived latency because it runs after the reply is sent.

kept.applies_to_our_stack: Applies directly. The bot already has its own agent loop on the same vLLM endpoint. This is about 150-250 lines of Python, roughly half a day of work.
kept.risk: Low to medium. The API key for Open WebUI has to be stored on the bot host; keep it local only and read-only for other scopes if possible. If the bot and the web UI review run at the same time, they may write duplicate memories. Mitigate by doing extraction in only one place, or by deduplicating on content similarity before adding.
kept.test_plan: Log cached_tokens per bot request with --enable-prompt-tokens-details. On turns 2 and later the cached prefix should cover at least the system prompt, profile and tools. Tell the bot a fact on Telegram and check that it appears in Open WebUI within 1 minute, and the reverse. Compare TTFT p50 over 50 messages before and after (expect lower or equal).
kept.verifier_reason: The design is sound and fits the stack. It costs no extra memory and the latency gain is real (a stable prefix, with volatile data moved to the end), and extraction after sending is a correct pattern. Two claims are inaccurate. Open WebUI API keys are not scoped: a key carries the user's full permissions (admin, for a single-user install), so 'read-only for other scopes' cannot be done. The exact Gemma-4 thinking switch is hedged correctly but unverified. The bot's sort order does not need to match Open WebUI's, it only needs to be deterministic. Running extraction in two places (the bot and Open WebUI's background review) is a real risk of duplicate memories, so it should be the default choice to pick one.
